claims.claim: Magic item and spell names are italicized and feat names capitalized, following the current D&D product style.
claims.source: Dragon Writers' Guidelines (Dragon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: names of magic items and spells should be italicized

claims.claim: A Dragon page holds about 750 words and submissions should not exceed 5,000 words.
claims.source: Dragon Writers' Guidelines (Dragon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: A full page of text in DRAGON contains about 750 words

claims.claim: Failure to present information in D&D styles is listed alongside poor writing and imprecise mechanics as a standard rejection reason.
claims.source: Dragon Writers' Guidelines (Dragon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: failure to present information in D&D styles

claims.claim: Backgrounds and stories accompanying new rules must be interesting enough to stand alone without their rules element.
claims.source: Dragon Writers' Guidelines (Dragon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: interesting enough to stand alone without their rules element

claims.claim: Steve Winter applied newsroom training to TSR text: game language must be direct and clear, avoiding flowery phrases and clever wordplay.
claims.quote: the language needs to be direct and clear

claims.claim: A rulebook must decide up front whether it teaches newcomers or serves as a reference for people who know the fundamentals; it cannot do both.
claims.quote: I don't believe it can do both.

claims.claim: Mearls frames the game writer as a documentarian of an imaginary world who focuses on the props of a story: locations, characters, creatures, past events.
claims.source: Mike Mearls of Dungeons & Dragons: Documenting Imaginary Worlds (SFWA, 2016-12-22)
claims.quote: The writer as a documentarian of an imaginary world.

claims.claim: Game writing dwells on the kind of exposition that would bore a novel, little of which appears as-is in play.
claims.source: Mike Mearls of Dungeons & Dragons: Documenting Imaginary Worlds (SFWA, 2016-12-22)
claims.quote: the kind of exposition that can make a novel boring

claims.claim: Mechanics demand a lawyerly precision of language while setting text deliberately leaves gaps for the players' imagination.
claims.source: Mike Mearls of Dungeons & Dragons: Documenting Imaginary Worlds (SFWA, 2016-12-22)

claims.claim: Mearls' 2013 Legends & Lore column: rules terms exist to give abstract concepts a clear shared meaning, so '5th-level wizard' tells everyone what you can do.
claims.source: Legend & Lore says 'story not rules' (EN World thread quoting Mearls' 2013-03-04 column)

claims.claim: Mearls contrasts a self-explanatory descriptor like 'archer' with abstract feat names (Rapid Shot, Precise Shot) that can only be understood by already knowing them.
claims.source: Legend & Lore says 'story not rules' (EN World thread quoting Mearls' 2013-03-04 column)
claims.quote: They don't stand on their own in a meaningful way.

claims.claim: Perkins says he almost always overwrites; his first Dungeon adventure was cut from 28,000 to 16,000 words.
claims.source: An Interview with Chris Perkins, designer of Warriors of Heaven (Mimir.net, 1999)

claims.claim: Perkins notes Planescape's slang was mostly absent from Warriors of Heaven and that he missed the pull-quotes that made those products fun to read.
claims.source: An Interview with Chris Perkins, designer of Warriors of Heaven (Mimir.net, 1999)
claims.quote: What I miss are the pull-quotes

claims.claim: Perkins recounts a 1992 Dungeon draft of 24,000 words cut to 15,000 as a cautionary tale about overwriting, and pitches Curse of Strahd's register as Gothic horror with a dash of dark fantasy.
claims.source: Curse of Strahd Interview with Chris Perkins (Fraternity of Shadows, Feb 2016)

claims.claim: Perkins: adventures are meant to be read, so DM-facing text should be entertaining and bring a smile to the DM preparing.
claims.source: Chris Perkins on Writing your own Adventures (D&D Beyond, 2018-04-19, Todd Kenreck transcript)
